Luis Conte

Cuban percussionist Luis Conte came to the United States in 1967 and has become an in-demand session musician as well as a touring artist with James Taylor, Phil Collins, and other iconic headliners. For many decades he has made his home in Los Angeles.
Luis was interviewed via Zoom on November 24, 2025 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive and I’m very pleased to have Luis Conte with me this afternoon – afternoon for me and you’re on the other coast, so thanks to technology we can sort of have a virtual handshake. Thank you for being here.
My pleasure, man. My pleasure.

Earlier today I caught a video of you – I think you might have made it for your website, I’m not sure. But it started off with you sitting in front of three conga drums and you were playing the 3-2 clave with your left foot, and then you started doing your thing on the congas. And I just wanted to point out that I really enjoyed it.

Oh thank you. Yeah. You know because all that Cuban – if I’m playing congas and I’m playing authentic Cuban rhythms it all relates to the clave you know that. So I figured do a little bit of independence, put the clave in the foot and do that. I’m not the only guy that does that, a lot of the younger guys do that all the time. You know.

Years ago I was doing an educational thing with a Latin band from Albany, New York and we were trying to prepare the students to hear them. And the teacher says well – and the clave of course came up. And I was listening to the band and sometimes I’m going where is it? No one is playing it in this particular song but I assume it’s still there in your mind?

Yeah it’s inside. If you grew up in that culture with that music, the clave is inside of you. It’s there. And we know, it doesn’t necessarily have to be a percussionist, you know the pianist – every one of us playing knows where it is. If they know this music you know, they really understand the music, the culture. It’s just a thing. It may be, you know, if we didn’t have a drummer right know and a bass player and a guitar player start playing some real funky stuff, you immediately go to [claps] two and four. It’s inside of you. You have to. To us, to the Afro-Cuban drummer and musician, the clave is that. It’s just like automatic you know.
Were you able to hear American music when you were around 15 or so? I had a conversation with Ignacio Berroa and he talked about trying to pick up American radio
stations and the gymnastics they had to go through with the antennas and all this. And I’m wondering about your experience.

Yeah well two things. One thing, my father was a doctor but he loved music. My whole paternal part of my family was totally musical. None of them are musicians but they all played for fun and they were doctors and professors. And my dad was a doctor and he loved big band music, he loved all kinds of American – I listened to, since I was a yeah little boy I listened to all the big bands, you know Tommy Dorsey etcetera etcetera. And Glenn Miller. He had everything. And up until when the embargo came, after that you couldn’t get any more American records. But -- and he loved Nat King Cole, Sinatra, you know, and my sister, this is just before Castro seized all that remained, so Elvis came along and what was it, Bill Haley and the Comets, she had all these records. Ricky Nelson – I forget now some of the others. Gene Vincent. She had all these records of all these guys. So I grew up listening to the stuff in the house, before the embargo thing happened. This is early – because I was born in ’51 so in ’61 or so, by the time I was ten, that’s when really things got really closed up. So my first ten years I was listening to this music, American music in the house. Then all of a sudden the embargo comes in and we can’t get any more American music and we don’t know what’s going on. We’re totally closed off from the world. And a friend of ours that had left Cuba with his family sent one of my friends a letter with a bubble gum card in it of The Beatles and I will never forget – the letter says, “Hey man, this is what’s happening now. These guys are called The Beatles.” Blah-blah-blah-blah. What is this? You know. So my dad, it just worked out that my dad had just bought a radio, a Russian radio or Czechoslovakian, I don't know where this radio was from. Portable. And I could get, I don't know the station, I never knew, but I would tune in and I would get this station that was in English – I never knew where it came from. I’m from Santiago which is south of the island, southeast. So I don’t think it was Miami or anything up there, it was too far. It could have been Jamaica or I don't know. But it was pop radio. So they played, you know The Beatles, The Stones, Motown music, Aretha Franklin, you know all these, a whole soup of you know the top ten of what was happening. So that’s my American music influence. And honestly, while I was in Cuba I paid more attention to that than our actual traditional thing.

That’s so interesting. I was wondering, because I was thinking of a question about that because from my standpoint the music that you were listening to, which I also loved, would be considered simpler than Cuban dance music and did that occur to you later on? That the music of your own country was more complex, or am I off base here?

Yeah, I mean once I got out here and I started you know getting into music and now we start dealing with Latin music, Cuban music, the first thing I hear is guys going – well is this three-two or two-three? For example. And I’m going what are you talking about? I

mean play what you were playing [claps]. I said no, no, no but so you realize, that’s when I realized man, a lot of people – I mean and I would hear other musicians go like yeah, Latin music, nobody plays one. That’s another common thing I would hear. But to me it was just like what it was. Because in Cuba I earlier said I didn’t pay much attention to it, I was paying attention to it by osmosis because it was around, you know. And my parents, the other thing about my parents is they loved to hear bands and see performances. And I went with them since I was a kid, they would take me. So I was able to see Benny More, I remember seeing Emile Tevu, we would see Celia Cruz and you know the greats before they left Cuba, before they passed. So I was around this whole – without even knowing it. And my grandmother, one of the roots, you know Cuban music has – definitely has serious African influence. Such a huge African influence. And it comes from these tribes that came in the slave trade such as Yorubas from Nigeria, the Congolese from the Congo, Bantus, and Abakus or Naniguismos. And I also got my grandmother, when I would go to Havana I would go with her to some of these religious things where it’s really the root of the drumming, the bata drums – and I was hearing this stuff, like I didn’t even know what I was doing, I was just a little kid, a little boy. But it’s going in here.
Yeah and it stayed, right? It came out later.
Oh yeah.
Yeah. There’s a quote I read from you. “Music is almost like food to Cuban people” which I thought was a strong statement.

Yeah. You know the situation in Cuba is really hard, right at this moment, and it’s been for years. There’s the Communism thing and the whole bit of freedom and the embargo. And now it’s getting super worse. But I did go back to visit in 2009 and 2010 and 2012. And man, let me tell you these people, I mean they’re struggling but at one point I literally said okay, can everybody just be quiet for a second? Because you know you walk down, you’re either at the hotel, the restaurant, the Latin -- they’ve got like a killing samba band. This is in Santiago you know, playing son. Then you’re walking down the street and there’s a trio in the corner and they’re going on, and there’s a rumba happening, and then you’re walking down another street and like the radio is blasting. And this goes on, it’s food man, that’s how they keep alive man.
I’m going to ask you to move your screen so that you’re a little higher in the – yeah – that way the closed captions won’t cover your face.
Oh okay. Is this better?
Yeah that’s perfect, and then we’ll just edit this out.
I understand from your website that your parents arranged for you to leave in 1967?
Yeah.
Can you tell me what the conversation around the dinner table was like leading up to that?

Well it didn’t start at the dinner table, it started while I was in a car with my dad. And my dad would make house – he was a doctor so he was making house visits. And sometimes I would go with him, for whatever reason. And Castro was over there when Mr. Castro or whoever is in power now speaks everybody listens. Nothing else happens. The radio, everything is on the speaker. It’s like big brother you know. The speakers are in the street. And he was doing a speech, and he says, “From now on the men from the age of 15 are in the military and nobody leaves the island. That’s what happened. And I’m sitting here in my dad’s car and immediately I’m going – you know I didn’t know anything about – I knew I wasn’t free. I knew – it was the music was telling me you know, really you know, because I couldn’t access this music I wanted to hear from the outside for example. And anyway so I told my dad, “Hey dad, did you hear that? I just turned 14, man. I’m never going to get out of here.” And he said, “Well we’re going to have to get you out of here. I’ve got to speak with your mom and she what she says.” “But,” he says, “don’t worry, we may not be able to go with you, you might have to go on your own, but we’ll be out of here in maybe like six months or so.” Which he knew wasn’t true and I thought it was true but I didn’t see my mom and dad until seven years later, until I was 22, or even spoke with them. Because there was no communications. It’s not like now you’ve got WhatsApp and I know some Cuban friends of mine talk to their parents who are at home or their grandparents left back there. I couldn’t communicate with these guys except for telegram or letters. Anyway so that’s what happened. So my dad, it’s a bit of an old story but I didn’t have a passport. Why would I get a passport if they don’t want you to leave? But my dad knew people in the government because he had helped a lot of people during the revolution. When the revolution happened Castro lied to everyone. We all know that. We thought he was the Messiah and he turned out to be a dictator once he took over. But during that revolution you know like my uncle and my dad, they were supportive of the revolution and my dad helped some guys, being a doctor, in the City of Santiago and these guys now were in the government and he was able to – I don't know how he was able to get me a passport but he got me a passport. And he got me an exit. It’s a blessing man. I mean I’m Christian and I believe in Jesus and God man, and I think they had their hand on me and got me out of there. Because anyway I was able to get a visa, an exit – and it’s funny because the excuse that I went – you have to have an excuse. Why is this young man leaving? Well he’s going to get an education. And the government’s going, “We have the greatest education in Latin America so they say, so where is he going to go study?” “Because he wants to study, it’s
not taught in the island” “Well what is that?” “He wants to be a Catholic priest. He wants to be in the clergy.” Yeah. “Oh okay, well granted.”
Did they expect you to come back?

Yeah, oh yeah yeah. The thing is yeah, he’s coming back. He’s going and he’s coming back to help our people you know, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah – we love the revolution blah, blah, blah. That whole bit man.
The whole bit.
Yeah. So I was able to get out.
When you finally got to Los Angeles did you – were you homesick?

Yeah. Oh yeah, man. There were times, you know I ended up coming to Hollywood because there was a third cousin of my dad that lived here. And they were wonderful and I was there during high school. But there were times where I said I want to go back. I really missed my family, you know my mom and dad and my sister. I never saw my grandparents on my father’s side, my father’s dad and mom, I never saw them again. My grandfather on my mother’s side had passed but my grandmother is the only one, my mom’s mom, she came when my parents did. But I left home, I wanted to go back. I wanted to.
Did your parents ever leave?

Yeah, yeah. So seven years later they were able to leave. The same way – I had to go to Spain. I flew to Spain and so did they. They had these “Freedom Flights” that would go to either Spain or Mexico I believe. And their flight went to Spain and in Spain they were there and by then I was a resident here and I claimed them and they came and we got back together. It was wonderful.
You had to work for it.
Oh yeah. It wasn’t easy.
Was there a point that you can think of that you decided that you were going to become a professional musician? Was it gradual or was there like a turning point?

It was – well I have to explain to you because I never thought I was going to be a musician. I’m a really late guy. A super late guy. I played music since I was a little boy. I played guitar also, I had lots of guitar lessons when I was in Cuba. I was able to learn how to play son and some things like that from traditional – yeah, a wonderful teacher. And I had conga, bongo, I didn’t have timbales, but guiro, maracas, I had everything. And I would play. And sometimes my parents would have parties and you know, Compay Segundo from – he was the singer -- one of the singers on Buena Vista Social Club. The guy that wrote “Chan Chan.” Those guys were friends with my dad. They’re all from Santiago. And these guys would come in the house and they would have these parties, and I just sit in there [scats] not even knowing. So I come out here, you’ve got to

figure this, man. This is a 15-year-old just detached from his world, in Hollywood. You know I’m just, I don't know, I was lost. I didn’t know what I was doing I was just floating around. I wanted to finish high school then I guess you’ve got to go to college. I don’t have any money so I can’t go to an expensive college, I just go to a city college. And I still wasn’t thinking of being a musician. I didn’t know what I was going to do.
Was there any course of study that you were pursuing just for something to –

I thought for a minute, since my dad was a doctor, I was going to go into the medical field. So I started taking biology and you know all these, physics and chemistry. And I did well. But there was something missing man. Like the student body, what do you call it – the Latin American student body association of Los Angeles City College, you know I started meeting all these guys and we’d have little parties. And then one day I go to class and the African American Student Association had an event. This was in the ‘70s when the African Americans were finding their identity, you know the afros and the dashikis and all that stuff. It’s beautiful man. And I heard congas man. And I went – pfoom – forget the class. I went in there, these guys were playing. And I went up to them and I says, “Hey” you know, “where did you get these drums, man?” They go, “Oh these are Valjes, we got them over there on Sunset and this and that blah, blah, blah. “Really?” They said, “Yeah, the phone number is right there.” On the drums they had little tags. So I wrote the phone number down and I says, “Can I play?” They said, “Yeah.” I gave it a whack man, and those guys go, “Man, you can play.” I said, “Well, I’m from Cuba man.” And that’s when I went – I found the drums man. That’s I found it. I went all right, I’m going to do this. Where do you guys play? Where does this happen? Where are all the guys? This and that. Vroom. It was like I became a vacuum cleaner of information just getting everything in there man. Super late. I was like 18, almost 19.

That’s really fascinating. I wonder if you had the experience, perhaps at the city college, where you were taking a music course and the professor started talking about Latin music, explaining it, and you’re sitting there thinking hey, I already lived this.

No it didn’t happen that way. It happened the way I’m telling you, but then immediately I said okay I’m taking some classes here, I’m going to – I knew a little bit of theory and solfeggio and things like that on the guitar, so I says I’m going to take some music theory, piano, you know beginning piano and percussion ensemble. And I would go and listen to the noon band, the twelve o’clock band I forget – there was a big band and I would go there and listen and then I eventually asked if I could sit in. I mean – and my musicians, Mr. Spano was one of my teachers. The mention of Latin music was never mentioned back in those days. It was just theory and there was big band jazz, jazz band, and they would play Latin tunes. You know.
If you went to sit in with this band you mentioned, and probably they were playing mostly – well I’ll make an assumption here, swing or perhaps some rock at the time.
Right.
How did you know what to do with a swing groove, and did you get the feeling that you were kind of intruding on the goings on?

No man. Maybe it’s because I listened to so much American music as a kid. I just – oh, [scats] it’s timbao – it’s what we call timbao in Afro-Cuban, but just swing it. That’s all it is. You know. But at that time I had never heard of Chano Pozo, I had never heard of any of this. I didn’t know anything man. I really didn’t – of any of the – I started finding out who – I never heard of Mongo Santamaria, I had never heard of Tito Puente, I had never heard of Patato Valdes. These are guys that had left. I knew Papin, Tata Guines, you know etcetera etcetera when I was a boy. But the guys that were out here – so I’m just, I don't know, I’m floating, man. You know.
I bet you had some revelations along the way. I mean at that time there was some hit records by those fellas. Like “Watermelon Man” and some of the more accessible tunes.

Yeah, yeah. And I started hearing all this stuff from other friends that knew about this, “Oh right, you’ve got to listen – Mongo,” you know, so-and-so, that I had met. I met -- another guy that was going to LACC also, his name was John Montealegre was his last name. He was an African-American man but with the last name Montealegre and he lives in Pasadena, and he had a set of congas. So we hit it off, and I would go and hang out with him with a couple of friends, you know young guys you know just partying Friday night, Saturday night, over at his house it was just like listening to music and other guys who were like I found out about Fania, the label Fania that was the big of what they call salsa now of Cuban music. The label is Willie Colon and Eddie Palmieri. I went to a park out here, Griffith Park that was guys would get together and play drums. And I called them “thunder drummers” because I was used to hearing – when you play in Cuba in a percussion ensemble is playing. You know you play with a bunch of conga players and you have a comparsa or something in carnival. I mean everything is organized. All the parts are organized. Over here it’s like a drum circle. You know over here you’ve got guys that just go [scats]. So I kind of went like well this is not quite happening. But one day there was a – I heard some other stuff under some other tree. And there was this Cuban dude and this Puerto Rican cat and he had a – this is how I found out about Fania – he had a cassette and he was Willie Colon. And I went, “Dude, that’s Cuban music.” And he said, “Well yeah, this is from New York.” I says, “But yeah, who is this?” He said, “Well this is Willie Colon.” I says, “Well where do you get these records?” And there was one – at that time, this was the ‘70s – one record shop that carried this music. And it was downtown L.A. called Doran Music. So I went there, whatever little money I

had I bought a Willie Colon record, I bought a Puente album, and I bought an Eddie Palmieri “Azucar Pa Ti.” I still have them. And it’s just – it was all happening man. But it just, you know for me to go into, if you play a little funk I’ll just figure something out. And I’ve heard the tambourines and I’ve heard all that before. I’ll say one thing I would know – sometimes if you listen to some songs – I can’t think of them now – sometimes the conga pattern was turned around as a Cuban would play it. You know and it was like [scats] and I would go okay, well – that’s not even right.
It sounded more like you were doing like what a tom-tom – drummer might do on their tom-toms.
Yeah.
Back end of the measure or something like that. That’s a really intriguing story. Can you recall the first time you made money on a gig and how much was it?
Oh man. I made 25 bucks. I found out about this – are you still there?
Yeah.

Oh okay because your picture is not moving. I think you froze for a second. Anyway, while being at LACC another friend of mine from Santiago said, “Hey man there’s this club down here on Vermont and – anyways and the club was called Chespeako and there was a band with, the leader was the conga player, his name was Chocolaté. I never found out his real name. He was really a dark, black Cuban. Chocolaté. They called him Chocolaté, and his wife Sylvia. And he had a timbale player, a bass player, piano player, he played the congas and Sylvia sang. It was a small group. And I started going there. I’d go in and try to meet them. I wanted to play. And I’d go, “Hey man, from Santiago, from Cuba you know, I just got here.” I lied a little bit, I says, “Hey man, I used to play in Cuba” you know I played with so-and-so. I just made shit up man. I said, “Oh yeah they’re probably looking at me like you little punk you know, don’t be jiving us man.
Yeah sure go ahead, take our gig.

Yeah sure man. Now that I thought about it this guy probably thought I was a fool man totally, I [inaudible]. Anyway so from that gig he said, I said, “Hey can I bring some bongos and sit in with you guys? You’ve got a conga player and a timbale player.” “Yeah okay bring them.” So I go down there and play bongos with them, you know for free, and Chocolaté one days says, “Hey we have a wedding on Saturday and I’m going to have a little bigger band, do you want to play bongos with us?” Man, I thought I was – I went “Yeah!” I didn’t even ask about money. He said, “Well it’s going to pay 25 bucks.” I go, “Psh, great.” I’m in man. So that was my first thing man, my first little gig. And it just started rolling from there. Things started happening.
They sure did. I’m going to fast forward a little bit but on your website and on you know Googling you, I went through the trouble of counting all the credits they had for you.
In the website?

Yeah, and also I just Googled it and I think I counted 67 and then it said, “and many more” of all the people you’ve played with. So I had a question about, there’s some Latin groups that did not have a drum set, but most of the time I’m guessing that you have a drummer and then there’s you. And is there a process of sort of negotiating with the drummer about how is this going to mesh?
Well my theory on that is like if now we’re talking about the Latin band?
Not necessarily. I’m talking about a lot of the studio work you do.

Okay. Yeah. I – if it’s a non-Latin thing, so it’s all the other work I do, most of the work I do, I’m the salt and pepper in the dish. And the drummer is the potatoes and the meat and the stuff. So I take a backseat. I try to stay – a lot of people say, “Man you and so-and-so play so well together, you and so-and-so play so well together.” So I’m just like finding my space without getting in his space you know. So I look at it that way. I’m not really taking a backseat but I just complement the groove of what’s going on in the music without being in the way of what the drummer is doing. It’s hard to explain but you’ve got to just take a backseat to that. If it turns around and we’re playing a Latin tune then I’m taking the front seat you know.
Yeah.
If I explained that right.
Yeah, yeah. That makes sense. And also it may depend somewhat on the form of the song. Is there any times where you just feel like my contribution here is to not play?

Oh yeah. Lay out or play something – you know you have a percussion set so go to another color. You know and I hear, maybe because I played guitar and I hear the chords. I don't know exactly where the chords are if I don’t have a chart or anything like that, but I hear the changes. I’m aware of all that when I’m playing. It’s very important to know that you know because it’s music. You know you’re beating on things but you’re playing music. James Taylor says, “Man, Luis Conte, he thinks and makes music. Well you know you’re part of the music so there are chords here and there are notes and there are – énfasis– how do you say that – you know I forget the word in English. But dynamics and all that stuff so sometimes you go to a small thing. It’s not all this. And also sometimes if you’re playing, let’s say you’re playing congas, you can’t really play, sometimes the traditional, even though it would be like the tumbao would work sometimes you don’t play as full as you would play it in a real Latin band because you don’t need all those eighth notes. That’s being over here oriented. You learn doing that, I learned that on doing a lot of sessions, doing sessions sometimes they’d say, “Hey man it’s a little busy.” I just cut back the sixteenths or the eighths. Or I say you’ve got [scats] so it’s a little busy, how about like [scats] that’s simple. And it makes sense.
You’re serving the song. You have to serve the song, correct?
You serve the song. The music is what rules. You are just adding to it.

Did you have a similar memorable experience with your first studio date? I mean you described your first paying gig really well. And do you recall the first time someone said we want you to record? You go, “Ooh, what’s that?”

Well my very first, first, first, first recording was with a Cuban Latin band, a salsa band you call now, it was with Camilo Azuquita he was a singer from Panama, of Cuban descent, that moved to L.A. and it was actually my first cool salsa gig in L.A. way, way, way back. And he wanted to record a 45, back in those days there were 45s, two songs. And I was the conga player in the band. And I went to the studio, I’d never been in a studio, I’d never seen this. And I realized that I play the congas and we needed somebody to play guiro, we didn’t have a guiro player. I said, “I’ll do it.” And I played over the track I had just played, you know, that thing that – I didn’t know you could do that.
Overdubbing.

Yeah. Overdub. So I overdubbed the guiro and then I overdubbed the maracas. And I went like, “I want to do this.” I love this. Yeah. That was my first experience man with Azuquita. But, so here’s the next thing though, so I had seen the recording studio. Now I’m going man, I hope somebody calls me for a session. You’re networking, “Here’s my number, man” you know blah-blah-blah. And I got a call, unfortunately I don’t remember who these guys were, but I got a call, it was for a TV show. It wasn’t a good experience, a TV show that was Journey to the Unknown or something like that, with Leonard Nimoy. It was a short – it didn’t last long that show. Leonard Nimoy was the host and he would talk about these weird things, supernatural things, whatever. And I get called, “Yeah we need somebody to play congas – can you bring some congas” you know. So I brought my congas and it was this experience of the red light went on and I played what I thought was cool, and they didn’t dig it. And they said it was either two busy or, I just, I froze man. I literally froze. I didn’t know what to do. So I wasn’t sure what to try to do so I just tried something else. That didn’t work out. Then we’d do it again, it didn’t work out. They said, “Okay, well thanks so much, Luis” you know. They gave me a check, “Really appreciate it man, thank you. Bye.” “Okay thanks, bye.” I get in my car, I’m driving out as I’m driving out I see another percussionist come in. It just broke my heart. So there is good experiences and bad experiences. I got nailed. So then I tried to find out what happened you know. And I called my buddy. So the guy that was coming in was a friend of mine, his name was Hector El Grade, who has passed now. And we called him Bucky. We became really, really good friends. We were already really good friends and I called him the next day I said, “Hey man I saw you coming into the studio, I was totally bummed out I just left, I was crying.” I said, “What happened, I don't know, did you do

that session?” He goes, “Yeah, yeah they just wanted this thing and you’ve just got to play simpler man.” He told me, “Man, this is not Cuban music. They didn’t want that. They wanted –” I went, “Oh.” So I just focus in and do it.
Sometimes the producers – if they don’t know the music they may have a hard time telling you what they want but when you play it, “Oh yeah, that’s what we want” but I can’t tell you.

That could have been it. And that’s probably, yeah. Because hindsight much later, now that I’ve had lots of experience recording I walk in a studio and I can tell if this guy knows what the hell’s going on or not. And I know how to play ‘em. I totally know how to turn them around and play ‘em. I’m not mentioning names but man there’s some guys that you think that would know, they have no idea. And you know a great producer really calls you because by now they know what you do and they let you do what you do you know. And they’re open to your ideas. And once you play, sometimes maybe you played something that they don’t dig and they may say, “Hey maybe try a different pattern” or “maybe that’s a little too busy” or something. Or maybe, “Do you have a different instrument?” But they let you come in and do your thing.
Do they give you a heads up about the session and say please bring X, please bring this and that.

On film work a lot of the times, yeah. Film work yeah. But on records yes, sometimes there is sometimes they may say, “Hey by the way do you have udus?” You know it’s this clay pot, you know it’s something special they would ask. Yeah, yeah. Okay, I think we’re going to need some of those you know. But I have a really good assortment of stuff that I send. So a lot of times I’m not really missing much of what they need. You know but at times they do ask for certain things, they may ask for a frame drum. You know, or an Irish drum, a bodhran or something like that. I’ve got it. “I’m glad you told me because I wouldn’t have sent it.”
I have a little story here from Don Alias.
Yeah.

I was able to speak with him and he had this story that he got a call to play with a Mick Jagger recording and he said, “I brought every piece of percussion I could get my hands on: littlest shakers, big drums, small drums, tambourines, a whole van load. I wanted to be ready. Turns out all they wanted me to do was play fills on a syn drum. You know? Boom. So I sat there for six hours going boom.”

Yup. Well I wanted to do a Madonna recording and I sent everything I thought, because it was for the movie Dick Tracy. I sent everything I own. And I ended up playing triangle. It was triangle on this one song [scats]. “Okay great, we got it, thanks Luis,” “Okay, see ya.” So you never know.
Do you get paid by the note?

Yeah. But you know you have to have – the other thing I learned early on is it’s not just one cowbell, it’s a whole bunch of cowbells. It’s not just one triangle, it’s a bunch of triangles. It’s not just one shaker, it’s a bunch of shakers. Because there’s a track – this particular cowbell may not really work with a triangle, do you have a different tone. You know. You learn, there’s a lot – you need a lot of stuff. Because you don’t know.
That’s a good quote. You need a lot of stuff.
Yeah man, we need a lot of stuff. I got a lot of stuff. I got so much gear I don't know what to do with it.
Do you have a cartage system? You know have people move stuff around for you?

Yeah. Angel City Drum Works is the name of the company and they have like – I think I’m the only percussion player they have, but they have a lot of drummers. Erskine, Peter Erskine, JR, a bunch of cats. And they take us around in the studios. But the new world now is having a home recording studio you know. So I have one and thank God I’ve been pretty busy about it, with it. And a lot of sessions happen now that you don’t go anywhere, you just do them here. Overdubs.

Yeah. They send you a track and you can add. Yeah. I have another quote here. I’m sure the studio scene, as you mentioned, has changed a lot. And this is from your James Taylor bandmate, Lou Marini. And he was talking about the way songs are put together these days, and he said, “When I listen to these vocoder vocals and the rhythm tracks you could just as easily be listening to a washing machine. Luis Conte is a master percussionist. He’s always playing stuff for us from African tribal music, Caribbean, Brazilian. It’s so much more complex. The grooves are so intense that it makes the electronic stuff seem stupid. It seems infantile compared to what humans do naturally.”

Totally agreed. Of course. Man, you know what I call – and I work on some of these, I could tell you some things that man, what are some of these, you know the modern music that you hear on the radio. It sounds like wallpaper music to me. That’s what I call it. I call it wallpaper music. It’s just wallpaper. It’s almost – you know do you notice the wallpaper? No? So, it doesn’t matter. There’s like a formula. And it’s not only sad man, you have this one artist becomes a huge hit, now you have every record company has their artist that is like that artist. What happened to diversity? That’s what’s going on now man. So you go back to the tribal stuff man. That’s why I play these guys all kinds of stuff. They love it. And Gadd and those guys. Yeah. It’s another world now. And the machines, you know what about this? I will go in and work on a song. If I’m doing it in my house that doesn’t happen. I play the first chorus, I play the second chorus, and I play the outro. But nowadays I’ve done sessions, big acts man, big artists. And you play the
first chorus, I play, let’s say I play congas, I play whatever, three, four, five instruments. “Okay we got it.”
I was afraid you were going to say that. They’re just copy and pasting, right?

Copy/paste. I said, “What do you mean you got it, man?” “Yeah, yeah, well” – I remember doing this one – I’m not mentioning who they were but they wanted something timbale fills. And I did the timbale fills on the first chorus. They says, “Okay we’re good.” I said, “Bro, you’re not good, I mean you’re going to play the same fills” I mean whatever. You know. You know you don’t have to argue with them. I’ll tell you another – you want to know a story that’s kind of crazy? I go in to do a session. And I had already – I knew who the horn players that were before me, there was a session before me with a section. It was Dan Higgins and Jerry Hay and the late Gary Grant and Bill Reichenbach. You know, those four guys that played on all the Michael Jackson, all the great stuff. And I know they had been there because I had been working with them earlier and they said no we’re going over there to work. So I said okay, I’m going to be there at 7. So I get there for my 7 o’clock session and I’m recording. And then they go, “Let’s take a break.” And in another room I hear horns. And it’s those guys are the horns that just – and I walk in and I go, “Hey, how you guys doing?” “All right.” “What are you guys doing?” He says, “Oh man, yeah, we just have the horn section – we’re lining up the horns.” I said, “You’re lining up the horns?” You know Michael Jackson’s “Thriller?” Those are the guys on that record. They didn’t line those horns up back then. You know horn players breathe a certain way. The reason why they call those four guys to do all these record dates that are so funky on Al Jarreau or Michael Jackson. Whatever, you name it. The reason why they call them is because it’s a section. And they breathe a certain way and they play together and it’s just the beauty of the thing. “You guys are lining this shit up? What?”
They’re lining it up?
Yeah they’re like.

I know what you mean. Because they can see the waveforms, they can literally like move something incrementally. Oh good Lord. in other words let’s take all the human feel out of this. It’ll be better.
There you go. That’s what’s up. That’s 2025.

You know people who aspire to this life they may not know that it’s partly gone, but I think they’re probably envious of what you and these other fellas you’ve mentioned do. Is there any downside or challenges that you’ve had to deal with with this life? Which is in the studios a lot but also then touring and so forth?
Well I mean it’s not an easy life man. The famous line is like you’re as good as your last phone call. That’s the real world. I mean I’ve done huge tours and you come home and

you’ve got to keep working so you’ve got to wait for the phone to ring, so you’re as good as – well if the phone doesn’t ring well oh yeah you just toured with Madonna, great. What have you been doing the last three months? “I’ve been doing nothing.” That wasn’t the case but it’s not an easy life. And the other side of that, the road thing, the session thing you just don’t say no first of all. You don’t say no to any gigs man. That’s my philosophy. I don’t say no. If I’m free I’ll be there. Then you go on tour and the touring thing, the one thing I enjoy being out there because I like seeing people and I like to feel the air moving when I’m playing, it’s a whole other thing. When I was really – when the studio work was really really super busy even having three sessions a day, guys would tell me, “Man what are you going on tour with Phil Collins?” “Well man, because I’m going to like take a break from this, being in this room, to like seeing the air move.” But you do miss your family. You know I’ve been blessed with a wonderful wife and I’ve known her – we go back from before the times with Chocolaté that how long we’ve known each other. And she’s been very patient. And she was a great mom, I’ve had a couple kids. So I’ve been really blessed with that. But it can be really hard on families.
Yeah I bet your kids –
Being on the road, so it’s not an easy thing.
Your kids probably learned early on what the word “gig” meant. Yeah, dad’s got a gig tonight again.

Yeah, yeah. I missed – well listen I missed my son’s birth – my wife was early and I was in Vegas. Luckily I was in Vegas so I just got home immediately. But I was out there playing and she was like two weeks early. And I was going to come home like three days later and I got a phone call “Paging” – in those days they used to page people in the casinos you know, “Paging Luis Conte.” And my dad’s going “You just had a boy.” I go oh man. So there’s an example. I wish I would have been there, but they understand. And they’ve come a long way. I’ve also been really blessed on having some great tours where I’ve been able to bring them along when they were young. My kids have traveled the whole world. Madonna used to allow the families, if you have kids bring the wife and the kids. We’d get on a plane and we’d just go. And Phil [Collins] also.

After you did like a couple of hundred studio dates I’m guessing that you stopped reporting on every one of them when you got home. I mean here in Central New York we don’t – if you do a studio date it’s sort of an event. And you come home and sort of say, “Hey how did it go.” What would really make you bring this up, what your date was like today to your wife or your kids. This was significant? What kind of date?

If I played on a song, if this is a record and I played on a song that I thought was really going to be a hit then I’d mention. I remember I played on an Eric Clapton song, it was called “Change the World” I think that was the name, “Change the World.” It was a hit.

And I remember going in, and the producer was Babyface. And I went to overdub. They already had – JR had played drums, Paul Jackson Jr., Eric was going to come in and play the guitar. And here’s an example of a great producer. Babyface would come in, says, “Hey check it out. Listen to the song.” He goes, “You know what to do.” So I went in there and did my thing. But the song was so great, I came home and I went like, “I think I just played on a hit song.” Eric Clapton. Okay. And another time it was, this is a more modern, it’s a girl, Colbie Caillat is her name. There’s a song called “Bubbly.” It was a huge hit when my daughter was just getting out of high school. And the weird thing was like I knew that song was going to be a hit. I could feel it. And I went in and I just mentioned it to my wife, “Hey I played with this girl, Colbie Caillat man.” And my daughter goes, “Colbie Caillat! She went to high school with me.” I go, “Really?” She said, “Yes.” “Well I did a song that’s going to be a hit.” And it was. But that’s rarely. I don’t talk much about it. If it’s like some, like Chucho Valdes came to town and I just played with him then I’d be talking about it. I’d be going, “Man I just played” I just played, and Irakere came (when Irakere was together) to play here in L.A. and the conga player did not get a visa. And they called me. I couldn’t believe it. I was like what? You want to hear what happened? I’ll tell you real quick. I was doing actually, they called me up and it was a show they were doing at UCLA. And I was actually in the daytime I had to do, I was working on a record with Sheryl Crow, who was another big star, right, and Hugh Padgham and them, and they says, “You’re going to get there by 6 o’clock, the show is at 8. I says, “Okay, yeah, I can get there” because the session usually goes until 5. But of course it’s a record so it’s not really going just right and I just went – at 5 o’clock I went like, “Hugh, I’m sorry Bro, I’ve gotta go. I’ll be back tomorrow.” He says okay, you know, blah-blah-blah. So I get over there and I’m so excited because Irakere man, I mean. And those guys are like backstage and I walk in and I was – I must have sounded like I was a groupie man, because I’m going like “Chucho, man I listened to this song, man I love you guys man,” this and that blah-blah-blah. Carlos DelPuerto, Emilio, and blah-blah-blah-blah-blah. And they was looking at me like okay. So no rehearsal, they had already sound checked. So I go up there and I started playing. The first song they played is “Mambo Influenciado.” And Chucho goes, “Hey when there’s a break coming up, you know, I’ll give you – just keep your eyes open you know.” “Yeah, cool.” I know all their tunes, man. So the song – we finished it, boom I nailed everything. Chucho stops the show and goes like – he stands up and looks at me and he goes like, “Hey, all that stuff that you were saying is true.” I’ll never forget that. But stuff like that, man, I would talk about that all day.

You know I went down your list, a little mind exercise, I said I’m going to see if – choose two people that you’ve played with, or bands, that seem the farthest extreme possible. So I chose Barbra Streisand and Rancid.
Yeah. Wow.
Right.
Check that out. No kidding. That’s crazy.
I mean what would Rancid want from you?

Barbara had a hundred piece orchestra. Rancid, they wanted me to play timbales. I don’t remember what else I played but I remember playing timbales with them. And they just wanted me to rock out, like you know, go man. Okay. Wow, that’s a good comparison.
Was it a live thing or did you have to do headphones?
Yeah.
Yeah I was guessing maybe a live thing you could really maybe rock out better.

Yeah, yeah. And they were totally cool guys. They were – you’d think these guys would be intimidating or something, they were very, very cool. We got along real well. I spent a day with them. But yeah, that’s totally like crazy.
It’s going to be on your mind later – Barbra Streisand and Rancid.
Wow. I’m going to write that down.

Well this has been a fascinating chat and I just wanted to end up with – it’s sort of a heavy question, but you came out of a society that you literally had to leave because of the government. And I’m wondering what you’re thinking of America in 2025 considering your experiences?

Man, it’s like a yin and a yang because I’ve been in socialism and communism and I know some of the government is going towards the left and I’ve seen that. But then I don’t like the other side of what’s happening also because it’s like, you know, the ICE thing and the – it’s just I don’t want to say fascist because I think it’s wrong when people mention fascism. But there’s things that are not right, what’s going on on the right side either. So it’s like two things and right now I believe none of them is good, none of them is right. It’s a serious mess. My wife and I talk about it. Like we have grandkids. I said man, we’re not going to be around much longer. I mean at the end of the thing. But my kids and my grandkids, I mean what’s the USA going to be like? You have all this division. It could be a civil war man. You know. I’m Christian and you’ve got the Muslims coming but then you’ve got this Christian guy – I just saw a thing in Michigan some guy insulting, going out of his way to insult – what’s up with that? That’s not being a Christian. You know. And it’s like this. And then the news networks, things are crazy man. They try to – I think they’re trying to divide us instead of put us together. Whoever
the powers that be, whatever, all these government things happening, they’re trying to divide us instead of being united. That’s the failure man, coming up. That’s my take on it.
Same conversations in our house, with our kids too. We’re having the same conversations, yeah.
Yeah man. It’s sad.
What’s next up on your calendar?

Well man you know I just released a record called “Ropa Vieja” with a really, really good friend and he’s from my area of the island. I’ve always been in LA – the tres guitar is not a very popular guitar. It’s the Cuban guitar. You know that instrument? Tres? And I always wished, man I wish there was a really good tresero in LA, and here this guy shows up, San Miguel, so we did a record together. So we were just trying to get that going more, it’s just so much fun. We just did a gig on a Monday morning -- this past Monday. And it was so cool, it was just tres, percussion, and a bass player. And we all sing. And tomorrow we’re getting together and we’re going to do a video. We’re going in the studio to do a video so we can get an EPK and get the things to get booked. So that’s – my next focus is like I want to do my thing now. I’m tired of all this playing for people.
You’ve paid enough dues, man.

Yeah man. And I’ve also got a seven piece band that – we sell out the Baked Potato, you know that club. And we want to get that going and just keep making music. And work, you know I’ll do sessions for people. But I’m more focused on the real thing now.
Right.
You know that – nothing better.
It’s like the music is still your food.

Man, you know, I don't know if you read this but I put this on my website. I don't know if this is on the website, but I had an interview and I didn’t come up with this line, but this guy wrote this line. He says “To ask me how long I’ve been playing percussion, playing music, is to ask me how long I’ve been breathing.” And it’s really it. Because since I was a little kid man, I mean I had pots and pans – I started with pots and pans and then the guitar. I just love it.
You know one day you might get a call from a producer and say, “Luis, can you bring like your pots and pans?”

Hey, that happened to me with Dr. John. We were doing a record with an artist named Willie DeVille and Matt was producing. And the first tune I go, “Hey man, what do you want me to play on this, man?” You know we were playing it live. He goes, “Man, you know what to do, this is pots and pans music.” I go, “Okay.”
And I thought I was making a joke.
Yeah man.
All right. Well I’ve really enjoyed this, and thank you for your time. Best of luck with your ongoing projects.
Yes, sir. I hope – where are you exactly in New York, right?
Yes. I’m in Rochester. Yup.
Right. Okay well I hope I get to meet you in person.
I hope so.
If we’re out there with James or something you’ve got to come out.
Yeah, I’ll definitely do that.
Please.
Thank you.
Thank you for inviting me.
All right. I’ll pause our recording here and we’ll say our good-byes.
All right.

segments.title: Copyright notice, biographical note and opening greeting
segments.summary: Archive boilerplate, a short bio note, and Monk Rowe welcoming Luis Conte to the Zoom interview.

segments.title: The clave inside Afro-Cuban musicians, and playing it with the foot
segments.summary: Rowe praises a video of Conte playing 3-2 clave with his foot; Conte explains the clave is internalized by anyone raised in the culture, even when nobody plays it.

segments.title: Listening to American records in Havana before the embargo
segments.summary: Conte's doctor father loved big bands, Cole and Sinatra and his sister had rock and roll records; all American music stopped with the embargo around 1961.

segments.title: Cuban music's complexity, seeing Benny More and Celia Cruz, and African roots
segments.summary: Conte realized in the US how Latin music is misunderstood; as a child he absorbed it by osmosis, saw Cuban greats with his parents and heard bata drumming at his grandmother's religious events.

segments.title: Music as food for Cubans, and return visits 2009-2012
segments.summary: Conte describes the hardship in Cuba today and how music is everywhere on the street, keeping people alive; a brief screen adjustment follows.

segments.chapter: Leaving Cuba and arriving in Los Angeles
segments.title: Leaving Cuba in 1967 after Castro's military decree
segments.summary: Hearing Castro's speech in his father's car, Conte was sent out alone at 14; the cover story was a wish to become a priest, and his parents did not see him for seven years.

segments.chapter: Leaving Cuba and arriving in Los Angeles
segments.title: Homesickness in Hollywood and reunion with his parents
segments.summary: Living with a cousin of his father in Hollywood, Conte missed his family; seven years later his parents left on a Freedom Flight to Spain and he claimed them.

segments.chapter: Finding the drums at Los Angeles City College
segments.title: Late start as a musician: childhood guitar and parties with Compay Segundo
segments.summary: Conte never planned a music career; in Cuba he had guitar lessons, played percussion, and watched friends of his father like Compay Segundo at house parties, then felt lost in Hollywood.

segments.chapter: Finding the drums at Los Angeles City College
segments.title: Pre-med studies at LACC and discovering congas at a student event
segments.summary: He began in biology and chemistry, then heard congas at an African American Student Association event, played them, and decided to pursue drumming.

segments.chapter: Finding the drums at Los Angeles City College
segments.title: Music classes and sitting in with the LACC noon big band
segments.summary: Conte took theory, piano and percussion ensemble and sat in with the college jazz band, where Latin music was never taught; he handled swing naturally.

segments.chapter: Finding the drums at Los Angeles City College
segments.title: Discovering Mongo, Puente, Fania and Los Angeles drum circles
segments.summary: Having never heard the exiled Cuban percussionists, Conte learned of Mongo Santamaria, Tito Puente and Fania records, found Griffith Park drum circles disorganized, and bought Colon, Puente and Palmieri albums.

segments.chapter: Finding the drums at Los Angeles City College
segments.title: First paid gig: bongos with Chocolate's band for 25 dollars
segments.summary: Conte talked his way into a small Cuban club band led by conga player Chocolate and his wife Sylvia, and earned 25 dollars playing bongos at a wedding.

segments.title: Role of the percussionist: the salt and pepper beside the drummer
segments.summary: Asked about meshing with drummers on sessions, Conte describes finding his space, leaving out notes, hearing changes, simplifying Latin patterns and serving the song.

segments.title: First recordings: Camilo Azuquita single and a failed TV session
segments.summary: His first recording was a 45 with singer Camilo Azuquita where he first overdubbed; his first studio call, for a TV show hosted by Leonard Nimoy, went badly because he played too busy.

segments.title: Bringing the right gear: Don Alias and Madonna stories, cartage
segments.summary: Conte discusses what percussion producers ask for, compares Don Alias's Jagger session with his own Dick Tracy session playing only triangle, and explains carrying many instruments via Angel City Drum Works.

segments.title: Modern production: wallpaper music, copy and paste and lined-up horns
segments.summary: Responding to Lou Marini's quote, Conte criticizes formulaic pop, home recording, and sessions where parts are copy-pasted and horns are quantized, as in a Thriller horn story.

segments.chapter: Life as a session and touring musician
segments.title: Life on call and on the road: missing family and his son's birth
segments.summary: Conte describes being only as good as the last phone call, never saying no, enjoying touring with Phil Collins and Madonna, and missing his son's birth while in Vegas.

segments.chapter: Life as a session and touring musician
segments.title: Hit songs worth telling the family: Clapton, Colbie Caillat, Irakere
segments.summary: Conte recalls overdubbing Clapton's Change the World with Babyface, knowing Colbie Caillat's Bubbly would be a hit, and being called to replace Irakere's conga player.

segments.chapter: Life as a session and touring musician
segments.title: Barbra Streisand versus Rancid: the extremes of his credits
segments.summary: Rowe contrasts Streisand's hundred-piece orchestra with Rancid, where Conte played timbales and rocked out in a day with friendly players.

segments.title: Thoughts on America in 2025 after leaving Cuba
segments.summary: Conte, having lived under communism, says both political sides trouble him, worries about division for his grandchildren, and Rowe shares similar concerns.

segments.title: Current projects: Ropa Vieja record, tres player and seven-piece band
segments.summary: Conte describes his new record with tresero San Miguel, an upcoming video, his band at the Baked Potato, and a quote that asking how long he has played is asking how long he has breathed.

segments.title: Pots and pans music with Dr. John and Willie DeVille
segments.summary: Conte recalls a record with Willie DeVille where Dr. John told him to play pots and pans music.

segments.title: Thanks and goodbyes
segments.summary: The two thank each other, mention meeting in person if Conte plays near Rochester with James Taylor, and end the recording.
